source.title: Eliminating Sharp Minima from SGD with Truncated Heavy-tailed Noise
source.authors: Xing-Yu Wang; Sewoong Oh; C. Rhee

record.file_problem: The supplied text is cut off during Appendix K.1; the main paper, experiments, and earlier appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares test accuracy and several sharpness measures after training with injected heavy-tailed noise and gradient clipping. This bears conceptually on whether a trained network property tracks generalization, but it does not test the claim versions’ specific setups or magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.gate_note: The reported image-classification comparisons are this study’s own results. Results from cited work are not included. The random-initialization gradient-noise diagnostics and hyperparameters are not outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization relationship to motivate and evaluate a new optimizer, but does not test V7's magnitude-aware measure. Its LB–SB comparisons hold update counts fixed rather than epochs, so they do not test V5's fixed-epoch claim. Partial label corruption does not supply V1's natural-label versus fixed-random-label comparison. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the empirical conclusion. The authors argue that clipped heavy-tailed SGD preferentially occupies wide attraction fields under their theoretical assumptions, and that their two-phase training methods produce flatter solutions and better test accuracy. They interpret the ablations as requiring both clipping and heavy-tailed noise in these settings. Appendix D describes sharpness and test accuracy as correlated and acknowledges counterexamples; the experiments do not establish a universal or causal sharpness–generalization relationship.
record.recipe_differences: The study injects heavy-tailed noise into SGD and clips gradients, then reports image-classification accuracy and sharpness. It does not use the random-label, width-sweep, optimizer comparison, dropout, large-batch, memorized-example removal, or magnitude-aware perturbation recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The heavy-tailed-noise method without clipping has much lower test accuracy on the reported SVHN and CIFAR10 tasks than the clipped proposed methods. On the CIFAR100 data-augmentation task, the reported 95% CI for Our 2 is wider than Our 1’s.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched update counts, LB has lower test accuracy than SB: 68.66% versus 69.20% on corrupted FashionMNIST, 82.87% versus 85.92% on SVHN, and 69.39% versus 74.42% on CIFAR10. The FashionMNIST reported confidence intervals overlap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large-batch SGD can reach lower held-out accuracy than small-batch SGD under a fixed number of updates after both have fit the training set.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed clipped heavy-tailed methods have higher mean test accuracy and lower expected sharpness than the listed alternatives. Augmented CIFAR10/100 experiments also improve accuracy; their sharpness results are declared omitted in rows_left_out.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested two-phase clipped heavy-tailed training recipes can improve image-classification accuracy and reduce unscaled training-loss sharpness relative to the tested baselines.

record.problems: Deep-learning comparisons cover three tasks in Table 1 and two data-augmentation tasks in Table 2; each reports averages over 5 replications, with 95% CIs in the appendix. The paper does not report training accuracy for the proposed methods in the supplied main text, and expected sharpness is measured only on training loss. The comparisons do not isolate a generalization gap at matched training loss. The loss-landscape theory is principally one-dimensional and assumes iid heavy-tailed noise; the paper notes structural conditions on the landscape.
record.rows_left_out: PAC-Bayes sharpness and maximal sharpness comparisons in Table A.3 and Tables A.5 are omitted; they are additional sharpness measures, but the 60-row cap is not reached. The paper also reports no separate test-accuracy outcomes for those metrics.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fully random-label training, near-perfect random-label fit, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy. Corrupting 200 of 1,200 FashionMNIST training labels does not establish this comparison.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning breadth, decoupled weight decay, and switching from Adam to SGD.
Batch-size effects under equal epoch budgets and adaptations that remove those effects. Table 1 matches update counts; Table 2 compares methods with the same small-batch size.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and removing dropout together with weight decay.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, and its ranking relative to norm- and margin-based measures. Appendix A's additional sharpness metrics also use unscaled perturbations.
Memorization-based example removal versus equally sized random removal followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All reported table values are correctly transcribed. The rows chiefly describe the study's own optimizer evaluation and should be retained as findings outside the specified versions, rather than claim-verdict evidence. The record's blanket statement that there is no large-batch comparison is incorrect: there is one, but its fixed-update budget does not meet V5. The supplied text ends during a technical proof, after the relevant experiments and discussion.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under tuning choices.
Large versus small batches under epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, weight-scaled perturbations, comparisons among similarly trained networks in one convolutional family, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.
